modalities.name: No Backstory Pickup
modalities.tagline: A drop-in game where nobody's job, past or story comes along.
modalities.whatItIs: No Backstory Pickup is a fast drop-in team game with one social rule: nobody asks or tells what anyone does for a living, where they are from or anything about their past. You know the other players only by their first name and by how they play today. The game is run by the players, with no captains or coaches.
modalities.coreIdea: Being known only by how you show up today, with no job, history or reputation attached, may feel freeing for people who are tired of being their story.
modalities.whatYouDo: Fifteen to twenty players meet weekly in a park for 90 minutes of full-speed play, with first names written on tape. Before, during and after the game, talk is about the game, the weather and the moment, and anyone who slips into backstory gets a friendly 'not here'. Some people play together for months before learning anything else about each other, and that is the point.
modalities.whoItsFor: People defined by a role, a diagnosis or a past they would like a break from, and anyone who wants to meet people without the usual questions.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and anyone who needs help or support must still be free to say so.
modalities.tweet: Picture a pickup game where nobody asks what you do, where you're from or what happened to you. In No Backstory Pickup you're known by your first name and how you play today. An untested idea for anyone who'd like a break from their own story.

modalities.name: Borrow Their Move
modalities.tagline: Copy one move from an opponent you admired, and credit them.
modalities.whatItIs: Borrow Their Move is a competitive team game with a ritual of admiration: after each game, every player names one opponent whose skill impressed them, and in the next game they must try that player's move and say whose it was. Admiring someone becomes something you act on rather than something you envy quietly. The games themselves are fast and hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Turning admiration into imitation, with credit given out loud, may soften envy and comparison and make learning from rivals feel generous rather than threatening.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams play a 60-minute game each week, and at the final whistle each player tells one opponent which throw, cut or mark they are borrowing. The following week they try it in play, and when it works they call out the lender's name. The lender often ends up teaching it after the game.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel envious of others' talents, and competitive players who want rivalry to feel warmer.
modalities.cautions: Hard competitive play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and borrowing should stay a compliment, never a way to mock someone's style.
modalities.tweet: What if envy turned into a compliment? In Borrow Their Move you pick one opponent whose skill impressed you, tell them you're borrowing it, then try it next game and shout their name when it works. A new idea for competitive people.

modalities.name: Rule Jam Games
modalities.tagline: A nonstop running game whose rules are voted in and out.
modalities.whatItIs: Rule Jam Games is a fast running game with no fixed rulebook: players start from a basic disc or ball game and vote new rules in and out as they play. There is no plan, no score kept past each round and no goal of getting better. One rule never changes: whatever is voted in has to keep everyone running.
modalities.coreIdea: Playing hard under rules you did not choose, and that may change again in ten minutes, is meant to be practice in going along with change without needing a plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: A group of 10 to 20 meets on a field for an hour of nonstop play with a few discs, balls and cones. Every ten minutes anyone can propose a rule, such as 'throws must be backhand' or 'two discs at once', and a show of hands decides it, so most players end up running under rules they voted against. Nobody keeps score beyond the current round.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sport too rigid or get unsettled when plans change, and who want to practice change somewhere it is only a game.
modalities.cautions: Constant running and improvised rules can lead to collisions, falls and strains, so keep two rules fixed (no contact, no diving), warm up, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: An idea for grown-ups who miss real play: Rule Jam Games. Start with a disc, vote a new rule in or out every ten minutes and keep running, even under rules you voted against. No plan, no stats, just a game that keeps changing under your feet.

modalities.name: Silent Signal Matches
modalities.tagline: Full-speed team games played without a single spoken word.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Signal Matches are full-speed team games, such as Ultimate, played under one extra rule: nobody speaks. Teammates coordinate through eye contact, pointing, timing and a handful of agreed hand signs, and even disputed calls are settled in signs. ACT works through words, metaphors and talk about values; this keeps all of the connection and none of the language.
modalities.coreIdea: Taking words out of the game means teamwork has to happen through the eyes and body, so people connect and cooperate without explaining themselves.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 90-minute session, the group spends ten minutes learning six hand signs, for example for 'I'm open', 'foul' and 'replay the point'. Games are then played at full speed in total silence, with a short spoken break at halftime to adjust the signs. The session ends with players sharing, out loud this time, what they noticed about teammates when nobody could talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talking draining or feel they always over-explain, and teams that want sharper teamwork without words.
modalities.cautions: Without shouted warnings collisions are more likely, so play no-contact, keep a whistle or a loud clap for emergencies, warm up properly, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested concept, and some people find enforced silence uncomfortable, so it should stay optional.
modalities.tweet: A full-speed team game where nobody says a word: you read eyes, point, time your cuts and settle calls with hand signs. Silent Signal Matches is a new idea for connection through movement, with all the talking taken out. 🤫

modalities.name: No Sorry Game
modalities.tagline: Mistakes allowed, apologies banned: the team just says 'next'.
modalities.whatItIs: No Sorry Game is a hard, fast team game with one banned word: sorry. After a drop, a wild throw or a missed block, players may not apologize or explain, and the whole team simply says 'next' and plays on.
modalities.coreIdea: Banning apologies and explanations for mistakes is meant to make errors ordinary, so attention goes back to the game instead of to blame.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for 60 to 90 minutes with the usual rules plus the ban, and anyone who says sorry or starts explaining a mistake jogs once around a cone, laughter allowed. Teammates answer every error with a clap and 'next'. In the closing circle, each player names one mistake they let go of quickly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who apologize all the time, replay their mistakes or brace for blame, and teams whose mood sinks after errors.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the ban covers mistakes only: a real injury or foul still deserves a word of care.
modalities.tweet: Drop the disc, throw it away, miss the block, and you're not allowed to apologize or explain. Your team just claps and says 'next'. No Sorry Game is an experimental way to make mistakes ordinary, at full speed.

modalities.name: All Hands Scoring
modalities.tagline: No point counts until every player on the team has scored.
modalities.whatItIs: All Hands Scoring is a team game with one scoring rule: a team's points count only once every player on it has scored at least once, and until then they are tallied but frozen. Strong players cannot carry the game alone, so the whole team talks, plans and shouts to get the disc to whoever has not scored yet.
modalities.coreIdea: When no point counts until everyone has scored, attention may turn to including the person who is usually left out, and being included stops depending on skill.
modalities.whatYouDo: Mixed teams of seven play a 75-minute game, and a sideline volunteer ticks a box for each player the first time they score. Once all seven boxes are ticked, the team's frozen points unlock and the boxes reset for another round. Teams keep calling out the names of who still needs a score, so the talk on the field never stops.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who usually feel sidelined in sport, and strong players who want to practice making room for others.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the attention on players who have not scored yet should stay friendly, never mocking.
modalities.tweet: What if your team's goals only counted once every single player had scored? All Hands Scoring turns a game into a loud, joint effort to get the disc to whoever usually gets left out. Strong players can't carry it alone.

modalities.name: Thanks for the Pass
modalities.tagline: Every caught pass gets the thrower's name and a thank-you.
modalities.whatItIs: Thanks for the Pass is a fast team game with one rule: whenever you catch a pass, you say the thrower's name and 'thanks' before you throw on. Over a game that adds up to hundreds of small acknowledgments, given at full speed and out of breath. Defenders and opponents can earn one too, for a clean block or a fair call.
modalities.coreIdea: Naming who helped you, many times a game, may build the habit of noticing other people's contributions instead of only your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for an hour, and every catch is followed by a quick 'thanks' and the thrower's name, kept up even when everyone is tired. A sideline volunteer counts the thanks, and the team with the most earns one extra point. The game ends with each player thanking one person for something specific.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to overlook help or credit themselves for shared work, and teams that want a warmer atmosphere.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Thanks for the Pass. Every time you catch, say the thrower's name and 'thanks' before throwing on, hundreds of times a game, even when you're gasping. The team with the most thank-yous gets a bonus point.

modalities.name: Wristband Dares
modalities.tagline: A small dare taped to your wrist, done mid-game.
modalities.whatItIs: Wristband Dares turns a weekly team game into a place to rehearse small acts of nerve: each player writes one personal dare on tape around their wrist, such as asking loudly for the disc five times or making a call they would normally swallow. A buddy on the team quietly checks it off.
modalities.coreIdea: Small, self-chosen dares inside a fast game may make courage something you practice with friends around rather than something you wait to feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 90-minute game, everyone picks a dare from a shared list or writes their own, tapes it on and tells one buddy. During play the buddy notices when it happens and gives a thumbs up, and at the end each player says whether they did it and how it felt. Dares grow a little bolder week by week, chosen only by the player.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who go quiet in groups, swallow their opinions or never ask for what they want, and who would rather practice that in a game than in a meeting.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and no dare should put anyone's body or dignity at risk.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Wristband Dares. Before the game, tape one small dare to your wrist (ask for the disc five times, make the call you usually swallow) and a teammate quietly checks it off. Courage practice dressed up as a pickup game.

modalities.name: Three-Step Stop
modalities.tagline: At full speed, a random whistle means: stop, breathe, go.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Step Stop is a full-speed team game in which a whistle, blown at random, means every player brings themselves to a stop within three steps, holds still for one slow breath and then plays on. Between whistles the game is played hard and fast.
modalities.coreIdea: Bringing yourself to a calm stop in the middle of maximal excitement, again and again, is meant to be practice in pausing when you are fired up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of seven play a 60-minute game, and a sideline volunteer blows the whistle six to ten times at random moments. On each whistle every player slows to a stop over three steps, breathes out slowly once, and play resumes from where the disc is. At the end, players say which stop was hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who act on impulse when wound up or say things in the heat of the moment, and anyone who wants practice switching from full speed to calm.
modalities.cautions: Sudden stops strain knees and ankles, so the rule is to slow down over three steps, never to freeze mid-stride; warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a game could stop you mid-sprint? Three-Step Stop is a hard, fast team game where a random whistle means slow to a stop in three steps, one long breath out, play on. Practice in pausing when you're fired up.

modalities.name: Three Disc Mayhem
modalities.tagline: A team game with three discs in play at once.
modalities.whatItIs: Three Disc Mayhem is a loose, chaotic team game played with three discs live at the same time, so nobody can see or manage everything that is happening. Rules are minimal and the mood is playful.
modalities.coreIdea: With too much going on for anyone to track, players may learn to stop trying to control the whole game and trust teammates to cover what they cannot see.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play 10-minute rounds on a normal field, and each team can score with any of the three discs, while a score with one disc does not stop the others. Players call out names constantly so that passes can find them, and nobody tracks the total score. A session lasts about an hour, with short breaks between rounds.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they must keep track of everything, at work or at home, and anyone who loves noisy, unpredictable games.
modalities.cautions: With several discs flying, the risk of being hit or colliding goes up, so use soft discs, play no-contact, keep your eyes up, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the chaos may feel overwhelming to some players.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a team game had three discs in play at once? In Three Disc Mayhem there's far too much to track, so you stop trying to control everything and trust your teammates with what you can't see.

modalities.name: Secret Mood Lifter
modalities.tagline: Each half, one player is secretly in charge of team spirits.
modalities.whatItIs: Secret Mood Lifter is a fast team game in which, before each half, one player on each team draws a card that secretly makes them the mood lifter. Their job is to raise teammates' spirits on purpose, with encouragement, energy and timing, without anyone knowing who it is. At the end the card is revealed and the team says what helped.
modalities.coreIdea: Deliberately trying to lift a group's mood, and seeing what actually works, may show that the atmosphere around you is something you can influence, not only something that happens to you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of seven play two 30-minute halves, with a fresh draw for the mood lifter each half. Everyone plays hard as usual, while the lifter looks for moments to encourage, celebrate or steady someone, without overdoing it. After the game the lifters reveal themselves, and teammates name one moment that helped.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel at the mercy of a group's mood, and anyone who wants practice in being a good influence on a team.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the role is about encouragement, never pressure on anyone to look happy.
modalities.tweet: Each half, one player secretly draws the job of lifting the team's spirits: encouragement, energy, a well-timed joke. At the end they reveal themselves and the team names what helped. Secret Mood Lifter is a new concept for shaping the mood around you.

modalities.name: Slow Motion Rounds
modalities.tagline: Every other round played in dramatic, narrated slow motion.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Motion Rounds is a gentle, silly team game in which every other round is played in exaggerated slow motion, like a film replay, while someone on the sideline narrates it like a nature documentary. The other rounds are played at an easy jog, so the effort stays moderate throughout.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving absurdly slowly in front of others, with everyone doing the same, is meant to dissolve self-consciousness and turn being watched into shared fun.
modalities.whatYouDo: Mixed groups of 10 to 16 play six 8-minute rounds over an hour, alternating easy jogging rounds with slow-motion rounds in which throws, catches and celebrations are acted out at a crawl. Anyone can join whatever their fitness, and nobody keeps score in slow-motion rounds. The session ends with a vote for the most dramatic slow-motion moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel self-conscious moving in front of others, newcomers to sport, and anyone who wants a laugh more than a workout.
modalities.cautions: Slow, exaggerated moves can still strain muscles or cause falls, so keep them within a comfortable range, never dive, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the jokes should be about the game, never about anyone's body.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: a team game where every other round is played in dramatic slow motion while someone narrates it like a nature documentary. Slow Motion Rounds is a new idea for anyone who feels self-conscious moving in front of people. 🐢

modalities.name: Moving End Zones
modalities.tagline: Every three minutes, the place you are attacking moves.
modalities.whatItIs: Moving End Zones is a team game in which the field keeps changing: every three minutes a timer sounds and two volunteers move the end-zone cones to a new spot, so the target shifts while you play. The rules stay fixed, so the only thing that changes is where the goal is.
modalities.coreIdea: Having the goal move without warning, while the rules hold, offers practice in re-orienting quickly instead of clinging to the old plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for an hour on a large field marked with spare cones, and on each timer the end zones move to one of six marked positions, drawn by card. Teams get ten seconds to re-orient and then play on from where the disc is. After the game, players talk about what they did when the goal moved.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are thrown by sudden change at work or at home, and teams that want more adaptable play.
modalities.cautions: Sudden changes of direction strain knees and ankles and raise the risk of collisions, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Every three minutes the cones move, and the place you're attacking is suddenly somewhere else. Moving End Zones is a new team game for practicing what to do when the goal moves halfway through.

modalities.name: Tethered Pairs
modalities.tagline: Play the whole game within arm's reach of a partner.
modalities.whatItIs: Tethered Pairs is a team game in which every player is paired with a teammate and must stay within arm's reach of them all game, cutting, defending and catching as a pair. There is no rope, only an agreement, and a lot of laughing.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying in step with a partner at speed is meant to train attunement: noticing another person's pace and intentions and adjusting to them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of eight, in four pairs, play a 60-minute disc game, and a pair that drifts more than arm's length apart gives the disc away. Pairs swap partners every 15 minutes, so each player tunes in to four different people. The session ends with partners telling each other one thing they noticed about how the other moves.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to run ahead of others or get lost in their own pace, and anyone who wants to feel closely in sync with someone.
modalities.cautions: Moving as a pair raises the risk of tripping over each other and colliding, so never hold hands or use a rope, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: You and a partner, within arm's reach of each other the whole game: cutting, catching and defending as a unit. Tethered Pairs is an untested idea that trades solo speed for a feel for someone else's pace.

modalities.name: Marker's Honest Minute
modalities.tagline: Compete hard all game, then swap honest notes with your rival.
modalities.whatItIs: Marker's Honest Minute is a competitive team game that ends in an unusual ritual: you sit down with the opponent you marked most and each of you gives the other one honest observation about their play and one about how they handled calls. The game before it is played hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Swapping honest, specific feedback with someone you just competed against may make giving and hearing criticism feel less threatening.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams play a hard 60-minute game in which each player marks the same opponent as much as possible. Afterward each pair sits apart for two minutes each way and follows a card (one thing you did well, one thing you could change, one fair moment I noticed), and the only reply allowed is 'thanks'. Pairs rotate each week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dread feedback or avoid conflict, and competitive players who want to compete hard and stay on good terms.
modalities.cautions: Hard competitive play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and feedback should stay about play and fairness, never about anyone's body or personality.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Marker's Honest Minute. Play hard against one opponent all game, then sit down together and swap one honest observation each way, answered only with 'thanks'. A new way to practice feedback, with the person who just tried to beat you.

modalities.name: Call for a Sub
modalities.tagline: Shout 'sub' any time, for any reason, and you're out.
modalities.whatItIs: Call for a Sub is a fast, intense team game with one firm rule: any player can call 'sub' at any moment, for any reason or none, and is replaced at once with no questions asked. Fields are small and the play comes in bursts.
modalities.coreIdea: Saying 'I need a break' in the middle of excitement, and seeing it honored instantly, may make it easier to speak up about limits elsewhere.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of 12 to 16 play short, intense games with a deep bench, and any call of 'sub' pauses play for the swap. Calling it is applauded, never questioned, and there is no limit on how often anyone calls it. The session closes with players saying whether they called it as soon as they first noticed they needed to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who push past their limits to keep up, find it hard to ask for rest, or feel they always have to be the one who keeps going.
modalities.cautions: Intense bursts strain the heart, knees and ankles and raise the risk of collisions and head knocks, so build fitness first, warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems or high blood pressure. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Anyone can shout 'sub' at any moment, for any reason, and is swapped out instantly to applause. Call for a Sub is a new idea: a fast, intense team game for practicing 'I need a break' while everyone else keeps going.

modalities.name: Unison Openers
modalities.tagline: Every session starts with the whole team moving as one.
modalities.whatItIs: Unison Openers start every team session with a short warm-up sequence that the whole squad performs in exact unison, counted out like a drill team, before any play begins. The sequence is learned once and refined over a season.
modalities.coreIdea: Some studies link moving in time with others to feeling closer to them, so a shared opening may help a team feel like one group before the first point.
modalities.whatYouDo: The team writes an eight-count sequence of warm-up moves (jogging, high knees, lunges, side shuffles) and learns it together, then performs it in a tight block at the start of every session, ending with one shared shout. A new move is added each month. The rest of the session is ordinary hard training and play.
modalities.whoItsFor: Teams that feel like a collection of individuals, and people who bond more easily by doing than by talking.
modalities.cautions: A shared tempo can push some players too fast, so keep the sequence moderate and build it up gradually, stop playing after any knock to the head during the session, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if every team session began with the whole squad moving in exact unison, step for step, ending in one shared shout? Unison Openers is a speculative idea for building closeness by moving together rather than talking.

modalities.name: Win Card Game
modalities.tagline: Each team writes its own definition of winning before kick-off.
modalities.whatItIs: Win Card Game is a timed, structured team game in which each team writes down its own definition of winning before play starts, such as 'everyone throws a goal' or 'we never argue a call'. The result is judged against those words, not just the scoreboard.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing your own measure of success, and checking it afterward, may loosen the grip of the one measure everybody else uses.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each team has five minutes to agree on two win conditions and write them on a card, which the other team reads aloud. They then play a timed 60-minute game with the score kept as usual, and at the end each team checks its card and declares whether it won on its own terms. Cards are rewritten each week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who measure themselves only by results, and teams that want to care about how they play as much as about the score.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Before kick-off, each team writes its own definition of winning ('everyone scores', 'no arguing calls') and is judged by that card as well as the score. Win Card Game is a hypothetical way to choose your own measure of success.

modalities.name: Read Their Plan
modalities.tagline: Guess the other team's secret strategy from how they move.
modalities.whatItIs: Read Their Plan is a team game with a hidden layer: before each half, each team secretly writes a one-line strategy on a card, and during play the other team tries to work it out. A correct guess at the break earns a bonus point.
modalities.coreIdea: Guessing other people's intentions from how they move, and then finding out how often you were wrong, may soften certainty about what others are thinking.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play two 30-minute halves, writing a secret plan card before each, such as 'always throw to the left side'. At halftime and full time, each team gets one guess at the other's card. Afterward players compare what they thought they saw with what was really going on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy strategy, and anyone who often assumes they know what others are thinking and would like to test it.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Read Their Plan. Each team secretly writes a one-line strategy, then spends the half trying to guess the other's from how they move, with a bonus point for a correct read. Mind-reading, checked against reality every 30 minutes.

modalities.name: Quiet Ones Call It
modalities.tagline: The quietest players lead; the loudest play in silence.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiet Ones Call It is a team game that flips who gets heard: the players who usually talk least make all the calls, choose the lines and lead the huddles, while the usual loud voices must stay silent. Who counts as quiet or loud is decided by the players themselves, privately, before the game.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving the floor to the quietest voices, and asking the loudest to follow, may let each group feel what the other usually feels.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 75-minute game, each player privately rates on a slip how much they usually talk on the field, and a volunteer names the three quietest and three loudest on each team. The quiet three call every play and settle every disputed call, and the loud three play in silence, using only signs. The roles are redrawn every week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rarely speak up in groups, people who often take over without meaning to, and teams that want more balanced voices.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and anyone who finds being singled out stressful can opt out.
modalities.tweet: What if the quietest players made every call and the loudest had to play in silence? Quiet Ones Call It is an untested team game that flips who gets heard, so each side feels what the other usually feels.

modalities.name: Rain Is the Reason
modalities.tagline: Go out because the weather turned, and feel all of it.
modalities.whatItIs: Rain Is the Reason is a hard, self-led running habit triggered by the weather: when it starts to rain, the wind picks up or the air turns cold, that is your cue to go, and the run is about feeling it fully. Rain on the face, cold hands and wind in the chest, the conditions people usually avoid, become the whole point. There is no route and no plan, only the weather and your breathing.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing to meet unpleasant weather head-on, and finding it bearable or even exhilarating, may make discomfort feel more like sensation and less like a threat.
modalities.whatYouDo: When the weather turns, you dress for it and run hard for 20 to 40 minutes on a safe, familiar route, letting your attention go to the rain, the wind and the cold rather than to getting it over with. Every few minutes you name one sensation to yourself, such as 'cold on the ears'. Back home you warm up properly and note one thing that felt better than you expected.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who brace against discomfort or cancel plans at the first bad forecast, and runners who want to feel more alive in their bodies.
modalities.cautions: Bad weather brings slips, cold and poor visibility, so never run in lightning, on ice or in storms, wear bright clothing, choose familiar routes, warm up properly afterward, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: When it starts raining, that's your cue. Rain Is the Reason is an untested idea: go for a hard run because the weather turned, feel the rain on your face and the wind in your chest, and find out how bearable it really is. ☔

modalities.name: Promise Mile
modalities.tagline: One small, exact promise to yourself on every run, kept.
modalities.whatItIs: Promise Mile is a running practice built on keeping your word to yourself: before one hard stretch of each run you make a single, exact promise, such as 'no walking until the bridge', and then you keep it or note honestly that you did not. Here one clear promise is made and kept, with no negotiating mid-run.
modalities.coreIdea: Making small, exact promises to yourself and keeping them is meant to build self-trust: the sense that when you say you will do something, you do.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 45 minutes, and before the hard section you say your promise out loud, keeping it small enough to be realistic. Afterward you mark a calendar with a tick for kept or a circle for not kept, and add no other comment. Promises grow only when most of the recent ones were kept.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often break promises to themselves, or who no longer believe their own plans.
modalities.cautions: A promise must never override pain, dizziness or illness, so build up gradually, stop when your body says so, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and a circle on the calendar is information, not a failure.
modalities.tweet: One small, exact promise before the hard stretch ('no walking until the bridge'), then a tick or a circle on the calendar, no comment. Promise Mile is an untested idea for people who have stopped believing their own plans.

modalities.name: Run It Wrong
modalities.tagline: A hard run where the only rule is not doing it right.
modalities.whatItIs: Run It Wrong is a hard run with no right way to do it: no form cues, no target pace, no route and no judging, and if you want to flap your arms, zigzag or sprint then skip, you do. The effort is real; the rules are not.
modalities.coreIdea: Running deliberately without doing it right may loosen the grip of perfectionism, since the only way to fail is to try to do it well.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you run for 20 to 40 minutes on a safe, quiet path or field, as hard as feels good and in whatever style takes you. Whenever you catch yourself correcting your form or checking your pace, you do something sillier instead. Afterward you note one thing you did 'badly' and enjoyed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Perfectionists, people who feel they must do everything properly, and runners for whom running has become a chore of getting it right.
modalities.cautions: Wild changes of pace and direction can strain muscles and joints, so warm up, choose even ground, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: No form, no pace, no route: zigzag, flap your arms, sprint then skip. In Run It Wrong the only way to fail is to try to do it well. An experimental run for perfectionists who are tired of doing everything properly.

modalities.name: Usual Route Backward
modalities.tagline: Run your regular route the other way round, and notice everything.
modalities.whatItIs: Usual Route Backward is a hard, steady run on your regular route done in the opposite direction, starting from the end and turning every corner the other way. The ground is familiar but nothing looks quite the same, and the autopilot that normally carries you round stops working. Each time, you also change one small habit of your day.
modalities.coreIdea: Reversing a routine you no longer notice may show how much of your day runs on autopilot and make other small changes feel possible.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run your usual 30 to 50 minute route in reverse at a hard, steady effort, looking for at least three things you have never noticed before. The next day you do one everyday habit differently, such as the way you walk to work or the order of your morning. You note which changes felt strange and which you kept.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel stuck in routines, and runners who realize they no longer see their own route.
modalities.cautions: A reversed route brings unfamiliar crossings and traffic from new angles, so take extra care at roads, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Run your usual route backward and suddenly you see it. Usual Route Backward is a new idea: same streets, opposite direction, three things you never noticed, then one everyday habit done differently the next day. A small crack in autopilot.

modalities.name: Same Loop Again
modalities.tagline: One short loop, run again and again, until only rhythm remains.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Loop Again is a deliberately monotonous running practice: you run one short loop over and over for the whole session. Coherence Therapy digs for meaning in what you feel, but on a loop with nothing new to see or figure out, there is nothing to interpret. Attention settles instead on rhythm, breath and effort.
modalities.coreIdea: When the route offers nothing new, there is nothing left to interpret, and the run becomes pure repetition and rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick a safe loop of 400 meters to 1 kilometer, such as a track or a park path, and run it again and again for 30 to 60 minutes at a hard, steady effort. You do not count laps or check splits, and when your mind drifts to the boredom you return to the sound of your breath and footsteps. Once a week is enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overanalyze, who want a simple practice with no decisions, or who are curious what happens when boredom is allowed.
modalities.cautions: Running the same loop, especially on a track, loads the same tissues over and over, so change direction every few laps, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea and the boredom is part of it, but stop if it feels distressing rather than dull.
modalities.tweet: What happens if you run the same short loop for 45 minutes? Same Loop Again strips away scenery, decisions and novelty until only rhythm, breath and effort are left. A new practice for overthinkers who want something simple.

modalities.name: Forecast Then Run
modalities.tagline: Predict how you'll feel afterward, run, then check the forecast.
modalities.whatItIs: Forecast Then Run is a running practice built around a prediction: before each run you write down how you expect to feel afterward, from 1 to 10, and after it you write how you actually feel. The runs themselves are hard and steady.
modalities.coreIdea: People often misjudge how they will feel after exercise, and checking your forecasts against reality may make your gloomier predictions about yourself feel less certain.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before three runs a week of 25 to 45 minutes, you note one number for how you expect to feel afterward and one word for why. After cooling down you write the real number. After a month you look at how far off your forecasts were, and in which direction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose predictions about their own feelings keep them on the sofa, and anyone curious how accurate those predictions are.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and forecasts that are always bleak are worth mentioning to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Idea worth testing: Forecast Then Run. Before each run, write down how you expect to feel afterward, 1 to 10. After, write the real number. A month of that shows how good (or bad) your forecasts about yourself really are.

modalities.name: Speech on the Move
modalities.tagline: Rehearse the words you dread, out loud, with a racing heart.
modalities.whatItIs: Speech on the Move uses a hard, steady run to rehearse difficult words: the conversation you dread, the request you keep postponing or the talk you have to give, spoken out loud while your heart is pounding. Here the words are already chosen, and they get practiced under pressure.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing hard words while the body is already activated may make the real conversation feel more familiar when your heart starts racing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the run you write down three or four sentences you need to say, then run for 25 to 40 minutes on a quiet route, saying them aloud at different points, especially near the top of climbs. You adjust the words until they feel natural even when you are out of breath. Afterward you note which sentence still feels hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a hard conversation, interview or speech coming up, and anyone whose voice disappears when they are nervous.
modalities.cautions: Talking while running hard can leave you breathless or dizzy, so ease off when needed, run where you are comfortable speaking aloud, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Rehearse the conversation you dread out loud while running hard, so the words get practiced with a racing heart. Speech on the Move is a new idea for anyone whose voice disappears when the real moment comes.

modalities.name: Least Favorite Run
modalities.tagline: Once a week, run the route or condition you like least.
modalities.whatItIs: Least Favorite Run is a weekly hard run chosen for being the one you would most like to skip: the steep hill you avoid, the windy seafront, the early slot. You choose it deliberately each Sunday for the week ahead, and the other runs stay the ones you enjoy.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing the thing you avoid, on purpose and in small doses, may shrink avoidance and leave you with proof that you can handle what you dreaded.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each Sunday you list three runs you would rather not do and pick one for the coming week. You run it hard for 25 to 45 minutes and afterward write one sentence about it. Once a route stops feeling like the worst, you cross it off and choose a new one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who avoid the hard version of things, and runners who only ever run their favorite loop.
modalities.cautions: Some routes are avoided for good reasons, so never choose anything unsafe (unlit, icy or isolated), build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Which run would you most like to skip? Least Favorite Run is a new concept: once a week you pick exactly that one (the steep hill, the windy seafront, the 6am slot) and run it hard. When it stops being the worst, it comes off the list.

modalities.name: Kilometer Body Check
modalities.tagline: Every kilometer, check three body signals and adjust on purpose.
modalities.whatItIs: Kilometer Body Check is a hard run with a deliberate check-in at every kilometer: you quickly score three signals (breathing, legs, and jaw or shoulders) and then make one small adjustment, such as softening the shoulders or easing the pace. Nothing is left to drift. The run stays hard, but you steer it from the inside.
modalities.coreIdea: Checking in with your body on a schedule, and acting on what you notice, may build the habit of reading your own signals before they become alarms.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 45 minutes, and at each kilometer marker, or every five minutes, you give breathing, legs and upper body a score out of three. If any score is high, you make one change, from slowing down to unclenching your hands. Afterward you note which signal you tend to miss.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who only notice stress or tiredness when it is too late, and runners who push past signals they could have caught earlier.
modalities.cautions: A check-in is never a reason to push on through warning signs, so stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Do you only notice you're exhausted when it's too late? Kilometer Body Check is an untested idea: on a hard run, every kilometer, score your breathing, legs and shoulders and make one small change. Reading your signals before they turn into alarms.

modalities.name: Panorama Pace
modalities.tagline: When effort narrows your focus, widen it to the whole scene.
modalities.whatItIs: Panorama Pace is a running practice of wide attention under strain: whenever effort narrows your focus onto the pain or a thought, you deliberately soften your gaze until you can see the whole scene again, edges included. Structure is minimal.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping your view wide during hard effort may stop discomfort from shrinking your whole world down to the next few steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a familiar, safe route you run for 30 to 45 minutes at a hard, steady effort while softening your gaze, so that you notice movement and color at the edges of your vision. Whenever attention narrows onto the effort or a thought, you widen it again to the whole scene. Open parks, beaches and riverside paths work best.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention narrows under stress, and runners who want to stay connected to where they are when it gets hard.
modalities.cautions: A wide gaze must never replace watching your footing and traffic, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: What if you ran with your attention as wide as the sky? Panorama Pace is a new practice: hard, steady running with a soft gaze that takes in the whole scene, widening again whenever your focus shrinks, so a hard stretch doesn't shrink your world.

modalities.name: Stretch the Good Moment
modalities.tagline: On a hard run, catch each good moment and make it last.
modalities.whatItIs: Stretch the Good Moment is a running practice of savoring: whenever something good shows up during a hard run, such as a cool breeze, a sudden easy stride or the view at the top, you slow your attention down and make it last. Vipassana watches every experience arise and pass with the same calm. This one picks out the good ones and leans in.
modalities.coreIdea: Deliberately lingering on good moments during effort may help them register more fully, for minds that tend to skip past the good and dwell on the hard.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 45 minutes at a hard, steady effort, and each time a good moment appears you hold it for 10 to 20 seconds: you name it silently, notice where you feel it and let a smile happen if it comes. You aim for five such moments per run. Afterward you write down the best one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention goes straight to what is wrong, and runners who finish every run remembering only the hard parts.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and it is not a way to push hard feelings away, which are allowed too.
modalities.tweet: On a hard run, whenever something good shows up (a breeze, an easy stride, the view at the top), hold it for 20 seconds and let it land. Stretch the Good Moment is a fresh concept: five a run, noticing the good parts too.

modalities.name: Let Them Pass
modalities.tagline: An easy run where everyone overtakes you, and you let them.
modalities.whatItIs: Let Them Pass is an easy, unhurried run on a busy park path, with one rule: whoever comes up behind you, you let them overtake, and you never chase anyone. The pace is conversational and there is no plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Being overtaken again and again, on purpose and without reacting, may loosen the habit of comparing yourself with everyone around you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you jog for 30 to 60 minutes at an easy pace on a route with plenty of other runners. Each time someone passes you, you notice any urge to speed up, let it go and keep your pace, perhaps with a nod. Afterward you count how many people passed you and how many urges you let go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who compete with everyone, strangers included, and runners who cannot go easy when others are around.
modalities.cautions: Easy running still loads the legs, so increase time gradually, drink water and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Everyone who comes up behind you gets to overtake, and you never chase. Let Them Pass is an idea for competitive runners: notice the urge to speed up, let it go, keep your easy pace. Proving nothing, on purpose.

modalities.name: No Task Miles
modalities.tagline: A long solo run with no task for your mind at all.
modalities.whatItIs: No Task Miles is a long, solitary, steady run with no job for the mind: no question to solve, no plan, no podcast and no mindfulness technique. Thoughts can wander anywhere, daydreams included, and nothing has to come of them.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving a busy mind a regular hour with nothing to do and no one to answer to may feel like rest, even while the body works.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run for 45 to 75 minutes at a steady, comfortable effort on a familiar, safe route, without headphones and with your phone set to emergencies only. If you notice yourself planning or problem-solving, you let it drift rather than chase it. Nothing is written down afterward.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds are always on duty at work or at home, and anyone who is never alone with their own thoughts.
modalities.cautions: Running alone and lost in thought carries safety risks, so use safe, familiar routes, tell someone your route and return time, avoid isolated places after dark, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if wandering thoughts keep turning dark, talk to someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: A long solo run with no task for your mind: no podcast, no question to solve, no technique, nothing written afterward. Daydreams allowed. No Task Miles is a new idea for one hour a week when your head is off the clock.

modalities.name: Stop for Anything
modalities.tagline: Stop for anything interesting; count stops, not kilometers.
modalities.whatItIs: Stop for Anything is a loose, playful run in which you must stop for anything that catches your interest: a dog, a strange door, a bird, a view. Instead of distance or pace, you count the stops.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting curiosity interrupt the plan, again and again, may shift attention from achieving to noticing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you run for 30 to 50 minutes at a moderate pace, and whenever something interests you, you stop, look for as long as you like and then run on. There is no route and no target. At the end you note your stop count and the most interesting thing you saw.
modalities.whoItsFor: People always rushing toward the next goal, and runners who have stopped seeing where they run.
modalities.cautions: Stopping and starting is easy on the heart but can leave you chilled in cold weather, so dress for it, watch for traffic when you stop, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: A dog, a strange door, a bird: in Stop for Anything you stop for whatever catches your interest and look as long as you like, then score the run in stops, not kilometers. A concept that swaps achievement for curiosity.

modalities.name: Carry One Question
modalities.tagline: Take one question on a hard solo run, and see what comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Carry One Question is a solo running practice that pairs hard effort with a single question you take along, such as a decision or a puzzle. It is part physical challenge, part private thinking space.
modalities.coreIdea: A hard run with one question in mind gives the mind room to turn it over while the body is busy, and some people find it looks different afterward.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before you go, you write one question on a card, such as 'what do I want from this job?', and leave it at home. You run for 30 to 50 minutes alone at a hard, steady pace, coming back to the question whenever your mind wanders. When you get home, you spend five minutes writing down whatever came up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think better on the move, and anyone stuck on a decision who wants a different way to approach it.
modalities.cautions: Being lost in thought on a hard run makes you less alert to traffic and terrain, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and big personal decisions may still need talking through with someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Carry One Question. Write one question on a card, leave it at home, then go for a hard solo run and let your mind turn it over. Write down what came up when you get back. Made for people who think best when their legs are busy.

modalities.name: Summit Shout
modalities.tagline: Run hard up every hill and shout at the top.
modalities.whatItIs: Summit Shout is a hard hill run with a loud ending to every climb: at the top of each hill, if nobody is close by, you let out one full shout, as loud as you like. Qigong regulates the breath quietly and keeps energy contained. This spends it, out loud.
modalities.coreIdea: A full-voiced shout after hard effort may give pent-up tension a way out that daily life rarely allows.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you run a 30 to 45 minute route with three to six climbs, pushing steadily up each one. At the top, after checking that nobody nearby will be startled, you shout one long sound or word, then jog easily down. Some people choose a word for the day, others just roar.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold a lot in, rarely raise their voice, or carry tension they cannot name.
modalities.cautions: Hard climbs strain the heart and legs, so build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems; shout only where it will not alarm anyone, and stop if your voice gets hoarse. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Run hard up every hill and, at the top, if nobody's close, let out one full-voiced shout, then jog down and do it again. Summit Shout is a hypothetical practice for everything you hold in all week. ⛰️

modalities.name: Stash for Yourself
modalities.tagline: Hide water and a note halfway, then run to it.
modalities.whatItIs: Stash for Yourself is a hard, solo run with a gift waiting halfway: before you set out, you hide a bottle of water and a note to yourself somewhere along the route, then you run to it, read it and run home. You are your own support crew, with nobody else involved.
modalities.coreIdea: Preparing something kind for your later self, then receiving it mid-effort, may be practice in looking after yourself the way you would look after someone else.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you walk or cycle part of your route beforehand and leave water and a short note (an encouragement, a joke or a reminder) in a safe, discreet spot. Later you run for 40 to 60 minutes at a hard, steady effort, collect the stash at the halfway point and read the note before heading home. You take everything back with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who look after everyone except themselves, and runners who train alone and would like a small moment of support.
modalities.cautions: Hard solo runs strain the heart and muscles and nobody is there if something goes wrong, so tell someone your route, carry a phone, leave nothing behind, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Hide water and a note to yourself halfway along the route, then go for a hard solo run to find it. Stash for Yourself is a new concept: drink, read what you wrote, run home. Being your own support crew for once.

modalities.name: Lamppost Vocabulary
modalities.tagline: Recall one word of a new language at every lamppost.
modalities.whatItIs: Lamppost Vocabulary turns a hard, steady run along lit streets into a language lesson: you carry a short list of words in a language you are learning and test yourself on one at each lamppost. The route is a grid of streets rather than open countryside, and the mind gets a small, absorbing job.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving a busy or worried mind a small learning game to play while the body works may crowd out rumination and leave you with something gained.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 25 to 40 minutes along lit streets, with ten new words on a card in your pocket. At each lamppost you recall one word's meaning, checking the card only at junctions, and on the way back you test yourself in reverse. At home you mark the words you knew.
modalities.whoItsFor: People learning a language, and anyone whose mind loops on worries when it has nothing to do.
modalities.cautions: Thinking hard while running makes you less alert to traffic, so use quiet streets with pavements, look up at every crossing, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Ten words of a language you're learning, one recalled at every lamppost, then tested in reverse on the way home. Lamppost Vocabulary is an idea for a mind that loops when it has nothing to do.

modalities.name: Invented Kingdom Route
modalities.tagline: Turn your dullest route into a world only you know.
modalities.whatItIs: Invented Kingdom Route turns a dull, familiar run into an imagined world: each landmark becomes a place in a story you build over weeks, so the bus stop is a border post and the hill is a mountain pass. The running is hard and steady, and the story is yours.
modalities.coreIdea: Building a private imagined world along a real route may make a dull run something to look forward to and give the imagination a playful outlet.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you run the same 30 to 50 minute route, and each time you add to the story: name a new place, invent who lives there, decide what happens on the climb. After the run you add one line to a notebook map of the kingdom. Over months the route becomes a world only you know.
modalities.whoItsFor: Imaginative people bored by running, and anyone who wants some play back in their week.
modalities.cautions: Daydreaming makes you less alert to traffic and terrain, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Imagine your dullest running route as a kingdom: the bus stop is a border post, the hill a mountain pass. Invented Kingdom Route adds a little story every run, until after a few months your route is a world only you know.

modalities.name: Same Time, Elsewhere
modalities.tagline: Run at the same hour as a faraway friend, then swap notes.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Time, Elsewhere is a hard solo run done at an agreed hour with a friend who is running somewhere else, in another town or another country. You never talk during it, but you know they are out there working as hard as you are. Afterward you swap one sentence each about the run.
modalities.coreIdea: Knowing that someone far away is doing the same hard thing at the same moment may give a sense of company in solitude, without the demands of being together.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you and a friend agree a start time and a rough duration, such as 40 minutes, and each of you runs hard on your own route. You leave the phone in your pocket until you finish, then send one sentence, such as 'windy, but the last hill felt good'. Over months the messages become a small shared diary.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with close friends or family far away, and solo runners who would like company without having to arrange a meeting.
modalities.cautions: Running alone carries safety risks, so tell someone your route, carry a phone, build up gradually, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: every Tuesday at 7, you and a friend 500 km away go for a hard run at the same moment. No talking, just knowing they're out there too, then one sentence each afterward. Same Time, Elsewhere: company in solitude. 🌍

modalities.name: The Can-Do List
modalities.tagline: Track only what your body can do, never how it looks.
modalities.whatItIs: The Can-Do List is strength training whose only record is a list of things your body can now do: carry both shopping bags up the stairs, get up off the floor without hands, do ten clean push-ups. There are no photos, no measurements and no mirror checks, and you set up every lift facing a wall or window. The program itself is strict and self-run.
modalities.coreIdea: Measuring strength only by new abilities may shift attention from how the body looks to what it lets you do in daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five or six lifts, and after each session you ask whether there is anything you can now do that you could not before. When there is, you add it to the list in plain words, such as 'lifted the full suitcase into the car'. Once a month you read the whole list from the top.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel self-conscious or critical about their bodies, and anyone who wants strength to be about what they can do, not how they look.
modalities.cautions: Without a mirror you lose some feedback on form, so learn the lifts from a qualified coach first, use safety bars or a spotter on squats and presses, keep loads moderate and avoid holding your breath, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and strong body image worries call for professional help.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: The Can-Do List. Strength training where the only record is a list of things your body can now do ('carried the suitcase upstairs', 'got up off the floor without hands'). No photos, no mirror checks. Strength measured in life, not looks.

modalities.name: Strong in Every Room
modalities.tagline: One hard set in every place in your life, every week.
modalities.whatItIs: Strong in Every Room takes one hard strength set out of the gym and into each place in your life: squats in the kitchen, push-ups in the office stairwell, lunges in the hallway, each taken close to your limit. The gym program stays strict, but over a week the same strong self turns up everywhere.
modalities.coreIdea: Putting the same hard effort into every room of your life may make the capable you feel like who you are, not someone who exists only at the gym.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alongside two or three normal gym sessions a week, you pick five places (kitchen, desk, hallway, park, a friend's house) and, once a week in each, do one body-weight set taken to within two reps of your limit, such as squats or push-ups. You tick each place off on a small card. Every month you add a new room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel like a different person at work, at home and with friends, and anyone whose confidence stays behind at the gym.
modalities.cautions: Hard sets away from the gym can strain cold muscles, so do a few easy reps first, use good form, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and in the gym use safety bars for heavy lifts; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if your strength didn't stay at the gym? Strong in Every Room: one hard set in each place in your life (kitchen squats, stairwell push-ups, hallway lunges) until the strong version of you shows up everywhere. An untested idea.

modalities.name: Covered Plates
modalities.tagline: Train alone with weights marked by color, never by number.
modalities.whatItIs: Covered Plates is strength training in which you never learn how much you are lifting: once a month a friend tapes over the numbers on your dumbbells or plates and marks them only by color, and you train alone, choosing by feel. You lift what is in front of you as well as you can, judged by how it moves.
modalities.coreIdea: Lifting without knowing the number may loosen its grip, so a lift is judged by how it moved rather than by what it seems to say about you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a month a friend covers the numbers on your home dumbbells or plate set, mixes the colors and keeps a private key. Two or three times a week you train alone, choosing colors by how your warm-up sets feel and noting only 'heavier', 'same' or 'lighter' for next time. At the end of the month the friend reads out the key, and you notice how it feels to see the numbers again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose mood rises and falls with numbers, on the bar, the scale or a screen, and lifters who have stopped enjoying lifting.
modalities.cautions: Not knowing the load makes it easy to misjudge, so ask your friend to keep every color within a range you can lift safely, use safety bars on squats and presses, stop any set that feels wrong, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What would lifting feel like if you never knew the number? In Covered Plates a friend tapes over the weights once a month and marks them by color only, and you train alone by feel. An untested idea for anyone whose mood rises and falls with a number.

modalities.name: Effort Dial Sets
modalities.tagline: The same lift at three, six and nine out of ten.
modalities.whatItIs: Effort Dial Sets is strength training in which each lift is done at three deliberately different effort levels in a row: one set at 3 out of 10, one at 6 and one at 9, with the same weight but a different number of reps and a different intent. You learn to set your effort the way you would set a dial. The plan is strict and written in advance.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing exact levels of effort, rather than all or nothing, may make it easier to choose how much to give in other parts of life too.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you do four lifts, each in three sets: an easy set you stop well before tiring, a moderate set, and a hard set that ends two reps short of your limit. Before each set you say the target number, and afterward you rate whether you hit it. Over the weeks you aim to land within one point every time.
modalities.whoItsFor: All-or-nothing people who either go flat out or do nothing, and lifters who never learned to go easy.
modalities.cautions: The hard set is close to your limit, so use safety bars or a spotter on squats and presses, keep breathing rather than holding your breath, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and get medical advice first if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Are you all or nothing? Effort Dial Sets is a new idea: each lift done three times, at 3, 6 and 9 out of 10, with the target said first and checked after. Learning that effort is a dial, not an on-off switch.

modalities.name: Two-Choice Sets
modalities.tagline: Two safe options before every set, five seconds to choose.
modalities.whatItIs: Two-Choice Sets is a strength session in which every set begins with a small, fast decision: you have two safe options, such as heavier or more reps, and must choose within five seconds, then commit fully. The plan around those choices is strict and written in advance.
modalities.coreIdea: Making many small choices quickly, and finding that most of them turn out fine, may ease the paralysis of needing the perfect decision.
modalities.whatYouDo: You write a plan of five lifts in which each set lists two safe options, such as '8 reps at your usual weight, or 5 reps slightly heavier'. Before each set you count to five out loud and choose, with no switching afterward. After the session you note which choices you would make again, and how few of them mattered much.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who agonize over small decisions, and lifters who stall while planning every detail.
modalities.cautions: Both options on every card must be within your safe range, so write them in advance with a coach's help if you are new, use safety bars or a spotter on squats and presses and avoid holding your breath, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Two safe options before every set (heavier, or more reps) and five seconds to choose, with no switching. Two-Choice Sets is a speculative idea: a strength session that doubles as practice in small, fast decisions.

modalities.name: Eyes Closed Bodyweight
modalities.tagline: Hard body-weight sets with your eyes shut, a rail within reach.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyes Closed Bodyweight is a structured session of hard body-weight moves, such as split squats beside a rail, wall push-ups and step-ups, done with your eyes closed. Without sight you have to feel where your body is, through your feet, joints and balance. TRE lets the body shake involuntarily; this is deliberate, controlled effort guided only by your inner sense of position.
modalities.coreIdea: Working hard and moving well with your eyes closed may build trust in your body's own sense of where it is, for people who feel clumsy or cut off from it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do five body-weight exercises next to a wall or a sturdy rail, first with eyes open, then with eyes closed, for 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 slow reps that end close to your limit. After each set you open your eyes and check your position. Over the weeks you rely less and less on the support.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel disconnected from their body or clumsy, and anyone who wants to trust their body more.
modalities.cautions: Closing your eyes affects balance, so always stay within reach of a wall or rail, clear the space around you, never use weights with your eyes closed, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and stop if you feel dizzy, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness; people with balance problems, recent falls, uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Eyes Closed Bodyweight. Hard sets of split squats, wall push-ups and step-ups done with your eyes shut and a hand near a rail, feeling where your body is instead of watching it. Building trust in your own sense of position.

modalities.name: Anger Gets One Set
modalities.tagline: When anger hits, it gets one planned, safe, hard set.
modalities.whatItIs: Anger Gets One Set gives anger a structured, physical outlet: when you are angry, instead of reacting, you do one planned, hard 60-second set of a safe exercise with a weight you know well, then decide what to do about the situation. The rest of your training follows a normal strict plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Having a planned, safe place to put the energy of anger may create a pause between feeling it and acting on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose one 'anger set' in advance, such as 60 seconds of as many clean goblet squats as you can with a kettlebell you know well, and practice it in normal sessions. When anger rises, you do that set at full effort, breathing out on every rep, then sit for one minute before deciding your next step. You note what you decided and whether it still seems right the next day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who snap, say things they regret or bottle anger up, and who want a structured option somewhere in between.
modalities.cautions: Strong emotion raises heart rate and blood pressure and makes people lift carelessly, so the anger set uses a moderate weight you know well, never maximal loads or a barbell without safety bars; keep breathing rather than holding your breath, stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and get medical advice first if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. It is an untested idea, and anger that feels out of control or leads to harm needs professional help.
modalities.tweet: When anger hits, it gets one set. Anger Gets One Set is a new concept: 60 seconds of hard goblet squats with a kettlebell you know well, breathing out on every rep, then one minute sitting before you decide what to do. A planned place to put the energy.

modalities.name: Useful Strength
modalities.tagline: Once a month, your training goes into a heavy job for someone.
modalities.whatItIs: Useful Strength is a strict, self-run strength program with one monthly outing: you use your strength to do a heavy, practical job for someone who needs it, such as carrying a neighbor's shopping up the stairs or moving a friend's furniture. The weeks in between are training for that job. Progress is measured in what you were able to help with.
modalities.coreIdea: Linking strength to being useful to someone may give training a purpose outside yourself and make getting stronger feel like a form of care.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five lifts that build carrying, lifting and pushing strength, using safety bars or a spotter on heavy squats and presses. Once a month you offer one heavy job to a friend, an older neighbor or a community garden, and do it with the form you practiced. You note the job in your training log.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find training self-centered or pointless, and anyone who feels better when they are useful.
